lists.text:
1. Adopt a municipal food-waste reduction plan with a baseline audit and annual diversion targets.
2. Launch curbside organics collection that separates food scraps from landfill trash.
3. Subsidize backyard compost bins and worm farms for residents.
4. Create community composting hubs at parks, libraries, and neighborhood centers.
5. Fund a food-rescue app or hotline that connects surplus food donors with nearby charities.
6. Enact clear donor liability protections for businesses and institutions that donate edible surplus.
7. Offer tax credits or fee reductions to groceries and restaurants that donate surplus food.
8. Require large food businesses to separate edible surplus for rescue before composting.
9. Establish school cafeteria share tables for unopened, unused food.
10. Run a citywide “plan meals, shop smart” campaign for households.
11. Promote free fridge-inventory and smart-shopping apps through city utilities and libraries.
12. Educate residents on the difference between “best by” and “use by” date labels.
13. Encourage retailers to create “last chance” discount shelves for near-expiry items.
14. Support dynamic pricing systems that mark down food as expiration approaches.
15. Ask restaurants to offer smaller portions and easy doggy bags by default.
16. Subsidize surplus-prediction software for restaurants and caterers.
17. Promote grocery markdown alert apps to help residents buy near-expiry food cheaply.
18. Create an end-of-market donation program for farmers markets.
19. Organize volunteer gleaning teams to harvest surplus produce from farms and orchards.
20. Build a compost exchange linking urban gardeners with food-scrap donors.
21. Offer free food-waste audits and toolkits to restaurants, hotels, and grocers.
22. Train commercial kitchen staff on trimming, storage, and repurposing techniques.
23. Provide grants for cold-chain upgrades at small retailers and food banks.
24. Create shared refrigeration and freezer space for food-rescue organizations.
25. Fund mobile food-rescue vans to collect and deliver perishable surplus quickly.
26. Support a network of community fridges and pantries with clear food-safety guidelines.
27. Coordinate surplus meal pickup from faith-based and community meal programs.
28. Reduce hospital tray waste through room-service ordering and portion controls.
29. Encourage university dining halls to use trayless service, flexible portions, and surplus donation.
30. Require city-permitted large events and caterers to have a surplus-food donation plan.
31. Pair stadiums and convention centers with food-rescue partners for event surplus.
32. Set hotel buffet waste-reduction standards and donation agreements.
33. Open convenient food-scrap drop-off sites for residents without curbside service.
34. Expand municipal composting capacity or contract with regional composters.
35. Develop anaerobic digestion for food waste with energy recovery.
36. Create regulated animal-feed programs for safe, appropriate food scraps.
37. Support dehydration or processing of surplus food into shelf-stable products.
38. Cut food waste in city-owned buildings and municipal cafeterias.
39. Use city procurement standards to prevent over-ordering and require surplus donation clauses.
40. Run a public food-waste reduction challenge with neighborhood and business prizes.
41. Train neighborhood “food-rescue ambassadors” to coordinate local donations.
42. Offer cooking classes focused on leftovers, batch cooking, and ugly produce.
43. Run an “ugly produce” campaign and encourage retailers to sell imperfect produce.
44. Add food-waste lessons and cafeteria audits to school curricula.
45. Help employers adopt smaller cafeteria plates and track workplace food waste.
46. Grant food banks funding for cold storage, staffing, and rescue logistics.
47. Build a volunteer driver network for short-notice food rescue pickups.
48. Host an annual food-waste week with events, workshops, and donation drives.
49. Use zoning incentives to site food-rescue, composting, and processing facilities.
50. Adopt variable-rate trash pricing that rewards households and businesses for diverting food waste.

44. Require caterers on city contracts to donate safe surplus and compost the rest.
45. Pilot smart bins or weight-tracking at drop-off sites to measure and improve participation.
46. Introduce pay-as-you-throw pricing that rewards households for reducing trash and separating scraps.
47. Support worker training for food-rescue handling, composting, and food-waste auditing jobs.
48. Create a local food-waste reduction pledge for restaurants, grocers, and institutions.
49. Map and publicize free food resources to reduce household discards during shortages.
50. Set city food-waste reduction targets and publish annual progress reports.
